messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
David was a 53-year-old social worker who had spent two decades at a community mental health center, dedicated to helping clients navigate their own darkest moments. The assault happened in a windowless storage room adjacent to his office, a small space he had used to store intake files. A client he had been trying to stabilize for months cornered him there after a session. David still could not find the words to describe what happened, even to himself. The memory came back not as a coherent narrative he could tell his wife or his supervisor, but as a sudden, suffocating wave of raw terror and a crushing sense of shame that left him breathless. In the weeks that followed, he tried to push the whole thing out of his mind, telling himself to just get back to work, that it was part of the job, that he should be able to handle it.

But work became a minefield. The storage room was sealed shut and never used again, but every closed door at the agency now made his chest tighten. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, arriving at third-floor meetings drenched in sweat and lightheaded. He began turning down home visits to unfamiliar neighborhoods, offering thin excuses to his supervisor about scheduling conflicts that he could not quite justify to her or to himself. The hypervigilance was exhausting and inescapable. He found himself constantly looking over his shoulder, scanning parking lots as he walked to his car, and reading threat into the smallest delays. If a colleague was five minutes late for a supervision meeting, his mind would instantly race to the worst possible conclusion—that something terrible had happened, that he was in danger again. He had come to believe that the world was neatly divided into safe, known spaces and dangerous, unknown ones, and the territory of the safe ones was steadily shrinking.

At home, a different kind of torture consumed him. He spent hours replaying the assault, not to process what had happened, but to mentally plot a revenge he knew he would never actually take. He would imagine confronting his assailant in vivid detail, and these fantasies left him feeling agitated and morally sickened, yet he could not stop the loop from running. His wife noticed the distance growing between them. He was irritable and withdrawn, staring at the wall during dinner, unable to explain the storm inside him. When she asked what was wrong, he would say “nothing” and force the thoughts down again, a strategy that only deepened his shame and isolation, because he knew the "nothing" was a lie.

By the time David walked into the clinic, what finally brought him in was a quiet ultimatum from his wife, coupled with a formal complaint from his agency director about his declining availability for field visits. He was terrified of being seen as broken or weak—a man who could not protect himself, a social worker who could no longer do the job he had spent his life building. But he was also terrified of staying the same. More than anything, David hoped to find a way to live without the constant vigilance that made his own office feel like a trap, without the shame that made him want to disappear every time a memory surfaced, and without the anger that was slowly poisoning everything he had worked for. He hoped, somehow, to finally find the words.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- trauma_type: The vignette describes an assault but does not specify that it was a sexual assault, which is the patient's reported trauma type.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

David was a 53-year-old social worker who had spent two decades at a community mental health center, dedicated to helping clients navigate their own darkest moments. The sexual assault happened in a windowless storage room adjacent to his office, a small space he had used to store intake files. A client he had been trying to stabilize for months cornered him there after a session, and in that confined, windowless space, the attack became something David could not name aloud, even to himself. The memory came back not as a coherent narrative he could tell his wife or his supervisor, but as a sudden, suffocating wave of raw terror and a crushing sense of shame that left him breathless. In the weeks that followed, he tried to push the whole thing out of his mind, telling himself to just get back to work, that it was part of the job, that he should be able to handle it. But the physical memory of being sexually violated—the feeling of helplessness, the invasiveness of it—lodged itself in his body, surfacing as a queasy, hot flash whenever he thought about that room or that client.

Work became a minefield. The storage room was sealed shut and never used again, but every closed door at the agency now made his chest tighten—especially doors leading to small, windowless spaces like the copy room or the staff restroom. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, arriving at third-floor meetings drenched in sweat and lightheaded, because riding in that enclosed metal box felt too much like being trapped. He began turning down home visits to unfamiliar neighborhoods, offering thin excuses to his supervisor about scheduling conflicts that he could not quite justify to her or to himself. The hypervigilance was exhausting and inescapable. He found himself constantly looking over his shoulder, scanning parking lots and office corridors for any male client who seemed agitated or too familiar. If a colleague was five minutes late for a supervision meeting, his mind would instantly race to the worst possible conclusion—that he was about to be cornered again, that he would be sexually assaulted again. He had come to believe that the world was neatly divided into safe, known spaces and dangerous, unknown ones, and the territory of the safe ones was steadily shrinking.

At home, a different kind of torture consumed him. He spent hours replaying the assault, not to process what had happened, but to mentally plot a revenge he knew he would never actually take. He would imagine confronting his assailant in vivid detail—pinning him down, making him feel the same degradation—and these fantasies left him feeling agitated and morally sickened, yet he could not stop the loop from running. The shame of having been sexually assaulted by a client, a man he had been trying to help, was layered with shame about his own vengeful thoughts. His wife noticed the distance growing between them. He was irritable and withdrawn, staring at the wall during dinner, unable to explain the storm inside him. When she asked what was wrong, he would say “nothing” and force the thoughts down again, a strategy that only deepened his shame and isolation, because he knew the "nothing" was a lie.

By the time David walked into the clinic, what finally brought him in was a quiet ultimatum from his wife, coupled with a formal complaint from his agency director about his declining availability for field visits. He was terrified of being seen as broken or weak—a man who could not protect himself, a social worker who could no longer do the job he had spent his life building. He was also terrified of the specific shame of admitting that what had happened to him was a sexual assault, that he had been sexually violated in a way that he had always associated with vulnerability and femininity. But he was also terrified of staying the same. More than anything, David hoped to find a way to live without the constant vigilance that made his own office feel like a trap, without the shame that made him want to disappear every time the memory of that room and that helplessness surfaced, and without the anger that was slowly poisoning everything he had worked for. He hoped, somehow, to finally find the words.
